generatedProse.concept-context: Across the School of Sport, self-regulated learning shows in how you drive a piece of work rather than just complete it. Students in sport and exercise science, coaching, sport management and sport therapy share a focus on performance and health, but judge evidence differently: lab data and testing, training and match analysis, policy and participation, clinical and rehab practice. Whatever the subject, a self-regulating student sets a clear question, chooses which methods and sources to weigh, checks part-way whether the work is building towards an answer, and evaluates the result against the standard.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport and exercise science students have four weeks to write the same physiology lab report on a VO2 max testing protocol.

Tom starts measuring and writing as the data comes in, with no goal beyond reporting the numbers and no check on whether the analysis answers the question, until the report comes back with a disappointing mark. Tom was busy throughout, but never stood back to monitor or adjust. This is working without regulating.

Amara begins by setting a goal: a clear interpretation of the test data, tied to the strongest physiological evidence, finished a week early. Amara chooses which analyses to run, checks at the halfway point whether the results support the interpretation, and drops a measure that is adding nothing. Afterwards Amara notes what to do differently next time. This is self-regulated learning: forethought, performance and evaluation, run on purpose.

Both students worked hard. Only Amara drove the process, and it is Amara who will improve from one report to the next.
generatedProse.summary: Self-regulated learning in the School of Sport means driving your own work through forethought, performance and evaluation: setting a question and strategy, monitoring whether the evidence is building, and judging the result against the standard. Whether your evidence is lab data, training analysis or participation figures, the process is the same. You can now explain it and see it at work in a student's approach. The next lesson turns to one tool of self-regulation: judging your own work against the marking criteria.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara self-regulating rather than simply hard-working?

items.text: She set a goal, monitored whether her lab report's analysis was building, and adjusted which measures she used along the way.
She spent more hours on the report than Tom did.
She started collecting her data earlier than Tom did.
She asked the tutor for more guidance before starting.

feedback.correct: That's right. Setting a goal, monitoring the analysis and adjusting the measures is self-regulation in action.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara DID with the process, beyond working hard.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara was self-regulating because she set a goal, monitored whether her analysis was building, and adjusted her measures. Extra hours, an earlier start or more guidance are not the point.
